column4: The section sets a well-mouth below against the Lord Most High; 22:45 describes ruined towns with abandoned wells and lofty palaces, placing low and high structures together in a landscape of collapse.
The section says the fall has a blindness of its own; after 22:45's ruined wells and palaces, 22:46 clarifies that the blindness is in hearts, not eyes, connecting heedlessness with the descent.

The section contrasts a man tumbling down with a person turned toward the highest; 67:22 directly contrasts one walking face-down with one upright on a straight path, making posture and guidance part of the same image.
The section depicts a ruin from which wealth cannot rescue a person; 18:53 says wrongdoers will see the Fire and know they are falling into it, with no way to turn aside.
The section's fall carries blindness toward Fire; 17:97 depicts people gathered blind, mute, and deaf on their faces, with Hell as their refuge.
The section warns of falling into Fire; 54:48 depicts disbelievers dragged into it on their faces, making the downward bodily motion explicit.
The section describes a downward fall that can follow heedlessness; 2:36 says Satan caused Adam and his wife to slip from the Garden and they were sent down, a fall caused by temptation.
The section turns from falling to an upward summons; after the descent in 2:36, 2:38 promises that following God's guidance will leave no fear or grief.
The section's falling danger includes being drawn away by another; 20:117 warns Adam that Satan is an enemy who would expel him from the Garden and make him wretched.
The section names a foot-snare as a secondary dictionary sense of root ص ل ي (B005); 7:16 depicts Satan waiting in ambush on God's straight path, a specific lure away from the safe direction.
The section's dictionary image of a foot-snare suggests a trap from which one must be kept away; after 7:16, 7:17 has Satan describe how he will approach people from every direction to divert them.
The section says the fall has a blindness; 7:27 warns Adam's children that Satan and his tribe see them from where they cannot see, recalling the Garden's deceptive fall through an unseen enemy.

The section names a foot-snare as a secondary dictionary sense of root ص ل ي (B005); in 12:33 Joseph asks God to turn him from the women's plot rather than incline toward it, a specific lure he fears being caught by.

The section depicts the mindful person being turned away from Fire; after Joseph asks for protection from the women's plot in 12:33, 12:34 says his Lord answered and turned their scheme away from him.
The section's secondary dictionary sense of root ص ل ي (B005) is a snare; 8:30 recounts a plot to seize, kill, or expel the Messenger and God's counter-plan, a concrete attempted capture that fails.
The section's companion nearly pulls someone toward Hell; 35:6 calls Satan an enemy who invites his own faction to become companions of the Blaze.
The section contrasts a summons toward the highest with a downward end; 31:21 describes people rejecting what God revealed even when Satan calls them toward the punishment of the Blaze.
The section presents a turn toward the Lord Most High and the mindful person; 87:9 says to remind if the reminder benefits, setting up who responds in 87:10.
The section depicts the God-fearing person as the one turned away from the Fire; after 87:9, 87:10 says the one who fears will take heed.
The section contrasts the mindful person with the wretched one; 87:11 says the most wretched will avoid the reminder, leading into the Fire in 87:12.
The section contrasts one who descends into ruin with the one oriented toward the Lord Most High; 79:37 describes the transgressor whose end is set out in the next verses.
The section's lower direction is a choice away from the highest; after 79:37, 79:38 says this person preferred the nearer life.
The section names Fire as the destructive end; 79:39 says the Fire is the abode of the one who preferred worldly life in 79:38.
The section turns the mindful person's face toward the Lord Most High; 79:40 describes the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from desire.
The section sets the downward end against the upward direction; after restraint of desire in 79:40, 79:41 gives the Garden as the refuge.
The section says wealth is given only in seeking the Lord's face; 18:28 describes people who call on their Lord seeking His face and warns against turning one's eyes toward worldly adornment.
The section turns the seeker toward the Lord's face; 6:52 describes humble people calling on their Lord morning and evening while seeking His face, whom the Messenger must not drive away.
The section says wealth cannot help at ruin and directs the giver toward the Lord's face; 28:88 says everything perishes except God's Face, clarifying the lasting object of that orientation.
The section contrasts disposable worldly wealth with seeking the Lord's face; 55:26 says all on earth will perish, setting up what remains in 55:27.
The section directs the giver toward the Lord's face; after 55:26 says all earthly things perish, 55:27 says the Face of the Lord of majesty and honor remains.

The section says the giver has no favor to repay and spends seeking God's face; 2:262 describes spending without following it with reminders or harm, a specific form of giving without an imposed debt.
The section's giver acts without expectation of repayment; 2:263 says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm, sharpening the boundary around sincere giving.
The section gives wealth to purify oneself and seek God's face; 2:264 warns that showy spending and reminders can nullify charity, the opposite intention.
The section's ascent is giving wealth toward the Lord Most High; 2:265 depicts spending to seek God's approval as a garden on elevated ground that produces abundantly, joining charity and elevation.
The section says wealth cannot arrest a fall; 2:266 pictures a person's garden destroyed by a fiery whirlwind when he is old and weak, a precise loss of provision that cannot be undone.
The section contrasts wealth given for purification with wealth that cannot save; 9:34 condemns those who hoard gold and silver instead of spending it in God's way.
The section links ruin to Fire; after 9:34's hoarded treasure, 9:35 says it will be heated in Hell and used to brand its owners.
The section says holding wealth cannot protect the falling person and commends giving; 3:180 warns those who withhold what God gave them that the hoarded wealth will be fastened around their necks.
The section turns wealth toward the Lord's higher face; 28:77 tells Qarun to use what God gave him to seek the Hereafter, connecting provision to a higher end.
The section says wealth cannot keep someone from a fall; after the counsel in 28:77, Qarun claims his riches came from his own knowledge, a self-reliance exposed by his later destruction.
The section contrasts worldly possessions with seeking the Lord Most High; 28:79 shows Qarun displaying his adornments, the spectacle that makes people wish for his position.
The section directs the reader toward a higher reward rather than wealth; after Qarun's display in 28:79, people of knowledge say God's reward is better for those who believe and do right.
The section says wealth cannot help the one who falls; after Qarun is swallowed in 28:81, 28:82 shows those who envied his position recognizing that God distributes provision as He wills.
The section says wealth does not save the person who falls; 34:35 depicts disbelievers trusting that abundant wealth and children mean they will not be punished.
The section's wealthy man cannot rely on his possessions; after 34:35's boast, 34:36 says God expands and restricts provision as He wills, displacing the claim of self-made security.
The section says wealth is given to purify oneself and seek God's face; 34:37 says wealth and children do not bring a person near to God, except faith and righteous action.
The section's upward direction leads away from Fire; 3:133 calls believers to hasten toward forgiveness and a Garden prepared for the mindful.
The section makes giving wealth part of the ascent; 3:134 identifies the mindful by spending in ease and hardship, restraining anger, and forgiving people.
The section says wealth cannot secure the person who falls; 64:15 calls wealth and children a trial, placing worldly possession beneath the great reward with God.
The section contrasts the generous giver with the one who falls; 64:16 urges obedience and spending and says the person protected from greed is successful.
The section's giver seeks a higher reward without a human debt; 64:17 promises multiplied reward and forgiveness for a good loan to God.
The section says wealth cannot help at the moment of falling; 63:9 warns believers not to let wealth and children distract them from remembering God.
The section's wealth is spent toward God before ruin; after 63:9's warning, 63:10 urges spending before death arrives and a person asks for more time to give.
The section warns that worldly wealth does not stop a fall; 63:11 says death cannot be delayed once its time comes, completing the warning to spend before it.
The section says the falling person's wealth cannot help him; 6:94 depicts each person returning to God alone, having left behind what was given and losing the intercessors once trusted.
The section exposes wealth as no protection at ruin; 19:77 depicts a denier boasting that he will be given wealth and children, the false security challenged in the next verses.
The section says no worldly possession secures the final outcome; after the boast in 19:77, 19:78 challenges whether the speaker knows the unseen or has a promise from God.
The section's falling man cannot use wealth to escape consequence; 19:79 says the boast will be recorded and punishment extended.
The section says possessions cannot accompany the person in ruin; 19:80 says God will inherit what the speaker claims and he will come alone.
The section says the most mindful person is kept away from the Fire; 39:61 says God saves those who feared Him and no evil will touch them.
The section contrasts a person kept away from Fire with the one who enters it; 50:31 says the Garden is brought near to the mindful, completing the other side of the destination.
The section says the fall has a blindness; 80:1 records a speaker turning away at the beginning of the blind man's encounter, making turning and sight part of the moral scene.
The section's image links heedless direction to blindness; 80:2 identifies the person who came as blind, specifying the bodily scene begun in 80:1.
The section says the pious person gives wealth to purify himself; 80:3 asks whether the blind man might become purified, adding the possibility that the turning-away scene in 80:1-2 obscures.
The section contrasts the one who thinks possessions make him secure with the one who seeks the Lord; 80:5 describes the self-sufficient person who receives attention.
The section opposes false self-sufficiency to purification; after 80:5-6, 80:7 says the speaker is not responsible if the self-sufficient man refuses purification.
The section describes two opposed directions of striving; 80:8 introduces the person who comes striving, the opposite figure to the self-sufficient man.
The section identifies the God-fearing person as the one turned away from the Fire; 80:9 describes the striving visitor as fearful.
The section says the mindful person will be kept away; 80:10 says the speaker turns away from that fearful visitor, a painful reversal of the right response.
The section names root ع ل و (B006) as a summons toward a high place; 3:64 uses that invitation form to call the People of Scripture to a common word of worshipping God alone.
The section's named root ع ل و (B006) makes coming a summons upward; 4:61 calls people to God's revelation and the Messenger, then depicts hypocrites turning away from the summons.
The section names root ع ل و (B006) for the call to come to a high place; 6:151 uses that call to gather listeners for the Lord's ethical prohibitions.
The section's call upward establishes a direction; after the invitation to hear God's commands in 6:151, 6:153 names God's straight path and warns against diverging roads.
The section contrasts one who turns away with one who faces the Lord; 24:48 depicts a group turning aside when called to God and the Messenger for judgment.
The section's upward direction is a response to guidance; after 24:48's refusal, 24:51 depicts believers hearing and obeying when called to God and the Messenger.

The section contrasts a failing structure with one grounded in righteousness and says the giver expects no repayment; 18:77 depicts a wall about to collapse being set upright, with payment explicitly waived as a possible alternative.
The section says the giver has no favor to collect; after the wall is repaired in 18:77, 18:82 reveals it protected the treasure of two orphans until they mature, explaining the unpaid act.
The section's axis sets descent against an upward turn; 14:24 compares a good word to a tree firmly rooted with branches high in the sky.
The section's upward path bears a lasting result; 14:25 says the good tree gives fruit at all times by its Lord's permission.
The section contrasts a stable foundation with a collapse; 14:26 compares a bad word to a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability.
The section's direction turns toward the Lord Most High; 14:27 says God keeps believers firm in this life and the Hereafter while wrongdoers are left astray.
The section's pious person is kept away from ruin; 40:45 says God protected a believing man from Pharaoh's people's evil plot.
The section makes Fire the end of a false direction; after the believer is protected in 40:45, 40:46 says Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening.
The section says a companion or leader cannot save the falling person; 40:47 depicts the weak and arrogant disputing in the Fire, continuing the fate of Pharaoh's people in 40:46.
The section depicts false elevation ending in a fall; 10:90 recounts Pharaoh and his people pursued into the sea and overwhelmed by drowning.
The section warns that a fall leaves no time to reverse course; after drowning overtakes him, 10:91 rebukes Pharaoh's late profession of belief after prior disobedience.
The section contrasts the fall with a warning that can still be seen; after Pharaoh's drowning in 10:90-91, 10:92 says his body is preserved as a sign for later people.
The section's upward path includes caring for the vulnerable; 89:17 rebukes people who fail to honor the orphan, the opposite of the section's charitable ascent.
The section makes feeding the hungry part of the ascent; 89:18 rebukes those who do not urge feeding the poor.
The section contrasts giving wealth with ruin; 89:19 describes devouring inheritance greedily, a concrete form of holding wealth rather than directing it upward.
The section says wealth cannot save and should be given for God; 89:20 describes excessive love of wealth, immediately before the earth is crushed in 89:21.
The section's falling image ends in destruction; after the rebuke of greed in 89:17-20, 89:21 depicts the earth crushed again and again.
The section connects ruin with Fire; 89:23 says Hell will be brought that Day, completing the crushed-earth sequence begun in 89:21.
The section says wealth cannot help the one who falls; after Hell is brought in 89:23, 89:24 has the person regret not sending good deeds ahead.
The section's upward path includes care for the orphan; 107:2 describes the denier of judgment as pushing the orphan away.
The section names feeding the hungry as part of the ascent; 107:3 condemns the one who does not urge feeding the poor.
The section's person gives wealth to purify himself; 107:7 ends by describing those who withhold even small acts of help.
